chapters.title: The Word of Blessing
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 1

1The word of blessing of Enoch, with which he blessed the chosen and the righteous who will be there on the day of distress, when all the evil and the wicked are removed.

2And Enoch answered and said — a righteous man, whose eyes were opened by God, who saw a vision of the Holy One in heaven, which the angels showed me. And I heard everything from them, and I understood what I saw; and not for this generation, but for generations far off, that are still to come.

3Concerning the chosen I spoke, and I took up my parable concerning them: the Holy One will come out, and the Great One, from His dwelling,

4the eternal God. And from there He will tread upon Mount Sinai, and appear with His host, and appear in the strength of His power, from heaven.

5And they will all fear, and the Watchers will shake, and fear and great trembling will seize them, to the ends of the earth.

6And the high mountains will be shaken, and the high hills will be brought low, and they will melt like honeycomb before the flame.

7And the earth will be submerged, and everything on the earth will perish, and there will be judgment on all —

8and on all the righteous. But for the righteous He will make peace, and He will guard the chosen, and mercy will be on them. And they will all belong to God, and it will go well with them, and they will be blessed, and the light of God will shine on them.

9And here — He came with ten thousands of holy ones, to carry out judgment on them, and to destroy the wicked, and to bring a charge against all flesh for everything that sinners and the wicked have done and committed against Him.

Notes

  • On this book and how it is rendered — 1 Enoch does not survive whole in the language it was written in. The complete text exists only in Ge'ez (classical Ethiopic); behind it stand fragments of Greek, and behind those, fragments of the Aramaic original found at Qumran. This rendering follows the fullest witness at each point and the notes say which one that is. Where the witnesses disagree about a word, the disagreement is the interesting part and is reported rather than smoothed away.

  • v1 "when all the evil and the wicked are removed" — the Ge'ez has the evil and the wicked, a moral pair. The Greek has all the enemies, a political word. The Greek then adds four words the Ge'ez does not: and the righteous will be saved.

  • v1 "the chosen and the righteous" — the Ge'ez joins them with and, making two groups. The Greek has no and: chosen righteous, one group described twice. Much of this book turns on who the chosen are, and the witnesses differ in the opening sentence about whether that is one category or two.

  • v2 "not for this generation, but for generations far off" — Enoch says at the outset that the book is not addressed to his own contemporaries. Whatever else it is, it is written as a document meant to be found later.

  • v4 "appear with His host, and appear in the strength of His power" — the Ge'ez says both, in that order, using the same verb twice. The Aramaic from Qumran preserves the second half — he will appear in the [might] of [his] streng[th] — and the Greek breaks off before either. An army and a display of force are two different pictures, and the Ethiopic keeps both.

  • v5 "the Watchers" — təguhān in the Ge'ez, egrēgoroi in the Greek: the wakeful or sleepless ones. This is their first appearance, and they are the subject of chapters 6 through 16 and the reason the book exists. The Greek adds a line here the Ge'ez does not have — and they will sing hidden things in all the ends of the earth — where the Ge'ez has fear and trembling instead of singing.

  • v6 "melt like honeycomb before the flame" — the Ge'ez words are maʿāra gərā, honey of the comb. Printed English Enochs say like wax, which is smoother and is what beeswax renders down to, but it is not the word. Three independent readings of the Ge'ez were checked on this and all three gave honeycomb.

  • v7 "the earth will be submerged" — the Ge'ez verb is wa-tesattam, to be sunk or flooded. The Greek has something else entirely: the earth will be split with a deep chasm. Two witnesses, two ends of the world — one drowns, one cracks open. This is the sharpest single-word disagreement in the chapter, and it is also the first casualty of a fluent translation: of three independent readings of this word, two gave submerged and then one of those two printed rent asunder in its English anyway.

  • v8 "they will all belong to God, and it will go well with them" — the Ge'ez carries the verse well past where the Greek stops, through prospering, blessing, and the light of God shining on them. The Greek instead distinguishes two groups the Ge'ez does not: peace with the righteous, protection and peace upon the chosen.

  • v9 "And here — He came" — the verse the New Testament quotes. Jude 14–15 attributes it to Enoch, the seventh from Adam, and quotes it closely: Behold, the Lord came with his holy myriads, to execute judgment against all and to convict all the ungodly. Jude's last two words are sinners, ungodly — the same pair in the same order that ends this verse in the Ge'ez. Jude uses a past tense, as does the surviving Latin scrap (Ecce venit), while the Greek witness here has the present, he comes. The Ge'ez verb is the perfect form, grammatically past, but Semitic prophecy regularly states a future event in the perfect as something already done, so the form does not settle the tense.

chapters.title: Observe All the Works in Heaven
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 2

1Observe all the work in heaven, how the lights in heaven do not change their paths, how each one rises and sets, each appointed in its season, and they do not overstep their command.

2Look at the earth, and think carefully about the work done on it, from the beginning to the end — how nothing God does changes, as it comes into view.

3Look at the summer and the winter, how the whole earth is filled with water, and cloud and dew and rain settle on it.

Notes

  • v1 "Observe" — the first word of a sequence running to the end of chapter 5. Four times the reader is told to look at something in nature — the stars, the earth, the trees, the seasons — and each time the point is that they keep to their orders. The argument being built is that people do not.

  • v1 "they do not overstep their command" — where the Ge'ez says the lights do not transgress what they were told, the Greek says they appear at their festivals. That is not decorative: the whole of 1 Enoch 72–82 is a solar calendar argued against the lunar one, and the feast days are set by the lights. The Greek makes the calendar argument here; the Ge'ez makes an argument about obedience.

  • v3 "the signs of summer and of winter" — the Ge'ez and the Greek both have simply summer and winter. The Aramaic from Qumran has the signs of each. A sign is something meant to be read. The oldest witness makes the seasons a text; the later two make them weather.

  • v2 "as it comes into view" — the Aramaic has a word neither of the others does: observe its works — the earth's own works, rather than God's works upon it.

chapters.title: The Trees That Do Not Shed
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 3

1Observe and see how all the trees look withered, and all their leaves are stripped off — except fourteen trees, which do not shed their leaves, but wait with the old until the new comes, through two or three winters.

Notes

  • v1 "fourteen trees" — the number is in the Ge'ez. The Aramaic from Qumran says instead all the tr[ees], all of them, appear withered, with no exception made, and the Greek here is a torn line reading only observe and see all the trees. Whether the exception is original or later cannot be decided from what survives.

  • v1 "wait with the old until the new comes" — the Ge'ez and the Aramaic agree on this clause, and the Aramaic supplies the reckoning: [their] lea[ves] remain [... until] two or three [years pass]. Where two witnesses this far apart in age and language line up, the wording behind both is likely close to the original.

  • On the shortest chapter — one verse, and the witnesses disagree about how many trees it is about.

chapters.title: The Heat of Summer
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 4

1And again observe the days of summer, how the sun is above the earth and right over against it. And you look for shade and shelter from the heat of the sun, and the earth burns with scorching heat, and you cannot walk on the ground or on the rock because of its heat.

Notes

  • v1 — there is no Greek for this chapter. The witnesses are the Ge'ez and a torn Aramaic fragment, and they agree closely: the searching for shade, the inability to walk on ground or rock, the heat. Where two witnesses this far apart in age and language line up phrase by phrase, the wording behind both is likely close to original.

  • v1 "observe the days of summer" — the Aramaic again has the signs of summer, as it did in 2:3, where the Ge'ez has days. The same difference twice in two chapters is a pattern, not a slip: one tradition is reading the seasons as signs to be interpreted, the other as periods of time.

  • v1 "you cannot walk on the ground or on the rock" — the Aramaic reads the du[st] and on its rocks. Dust, not ground. It is the word from Genesis 2:7, the stuff the first man was made of, and the sun makes it untouchable.

chapters.title: But You Have Not Held Fast
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 5

1Observe how the trees cover themselves with green leaves and bear fruit. Understand about all of it, and know that He who lives forever made them all for you, and that all their fruit is for honor and glory.

2And His works are before Him year by year as they come, and all His works serve Him and do not change — but just as God ordained, so everything is done.

3And see how the seas and the rivers alike carry out their tasks, and do not change their works from His word.

4But you — you have not held fast, and you have not kept the commandment of the Lord. You have turned aside, and you have spoken against Him slanderously, great and hard words, with your unclean mouth, against His greatness. You hard-hearted: there will be no peace for you.

5And because of this you will curse your days, and the years of your life will perish, and the everlasting curse will grow, and you will find no mercy.

6And in those days you will make your peace an everlasting curse to all the righteous, and you will be cursed by sinners without end — you, together with the sinners.

7And for the chosen there will be light and joy and peace, and they will inherit the earth. But for you, the wicked, there will be a curse.

8And then wisdom will be given to the chosen, and they will all live and will never sin again, not through godlessness and not through pride. Those who have wisdom will be humble.

9And they will not sin again, and they will not be condemned all the days of their life, and they will not die by plague or by wrath. They will complete the number of the days of their life, and their life will grow in peace, and the years of their joy will increase in gladness and in peace forever, through all the days of their life.

Notes

  • v1 "all their fruit is for honor and glory" — the point the whole nature sequence has been building to. The fruit is not for eating; it is for honor. Obedience is being described as a kind of beauty. The clause is in the Greek and, broken, in the Aramaic (for maj]estic splen[dor).

  • v4 "you have spoken against Him slanderously" — the charge, and the reason for everything that follows. Three witnesses carry it and they line up almost phrase for phrase; the Aramaic has But you have changed your works [... and have spo]ken against him great and harsh words with the mouth of your impurity; [... hearts,] there will be no peace for you. Where a Dead Sea fragment and a Ge'ez manuscript a thousand years apart agree this closely, the wording behind both is near the original.

  • v4 "there is no peace for you" — a refrain in this book, and it lands on the accused rather than on their circumstances. Nothing is said about what will happen to them. It is said about what they are.

  • v6 "you will be cursed by sinners without end" — the Ge'ez says the sinners curse them. The Greek says something sharper: all the sinners and ungodly will swear by you — your name becomes an oath formula. A name used in an oath is a name people trust, and the curse is that these names stay in use, as the standard of what a wrecked life looks like.

  • v8 "Those who have wisdom will be humble" — the Ge'ez ends the verse there. The Greek runs much longer: in the enlightened man there will be light, and in the understanding man, insight. Both are saying that wisdom, once given, cannot be boasted about. They are not saying it with the same words.

  • v9 "they will complete the number of the days of their life" — the promise is not immortality. It is that the count runs out on time. Against the next chapter, where two hundred beings come down and ruin exactly this, it is the argument of the book stated in advance.

chapters.title: They Called It Mount Hermon
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 6

1And it came to pass, when the sons of men had multiplied in those days, that beautiful daughters were born to them, and lovely.

2And the angels, the sons of heaven, saw them and desired them, and said to one another, "Come, let us choose wives for ourselves from the sons of men, and let us father children for ourselves."

3And Semyaza, who was their leader, said to them, "I am afraid you will not want this deed done, and I alone will pay the penalty for this great sin."

4And they all answered him and said, "Let us all swear an oath, and bind ourselves to one another under a curse, that we will not turn back from this plan, but will carry this plan out in fact."

5Then they all swore together, and all bound themselves to one another under a curse upon it.

6And they were two hundred in all, and they came down onto Ardis, which is the summit of Mount Hermon. And they called it Mount Hermon, because they had sworn upon it and bound themselves under mutual curses.

7And these are the names of their chiefs: Semyaza, who was their leader, Urakibarameel, Akibeel, Tamiel, Ramuel, Danel, Ezeqeel, Saraquyal, Asael, Armaros, Batarael, Ananel, Zaqeel, Samsapeel, Satarel, Turel, Yomyael, Arazyal.

8These are the chiefs of the two hundred angels — the chiefs of the tens.

Notes

  • v1 "when the sons of men had multiplied... beautiful daughters were born to them" — this is Genesis 6:1 almost word for word: And it came to pass, when men began to multiply on the face of the ground, and daughters were born to them. Genesis gives the episode four verses and moves on to the flood. 1 Enoch gives it ten chapters. Whichever direction the borrowing ran, the two books tell the same story and only one of them explains it.

  • v2 "the angels, the sons of heaven" — Genesis 6:2 calls them bene ha-Elohim, the sons of God, and says nothing more about who they are. This book calls them angels in its second sentence on the subject and never treats the question as open.

  • v3 "I alone will pay the penalty" — the leader's objection is not that the plan is wrong. It is that he will be left holding it. The oath in the next verse is his fix: make everyone equally guilty. The book's account of how a group does something none of them would do alone is four verses long and has not dated.

  • v6 "they called it Mount Hermon, because they had sworn upon it" — the Ge'ez explains the name outright, and the explanation only works in a Semitic language. Hebrew cherem means something placed under a ban or a binding curse; that is the word for what the two hundred have just done to each other in vv4–5. So the mountain is named for the oath sworn on it. The Greek witness names Mount Hermoniem but does not give the etymology, and the Aramaic fragment breaks off just before the name. The complete Ethiopic text preserves a wordplay reaching back through a language it is not written in.

  • v6 "Ardis" — the Ge'ez treats Ardis not as an alternative to Hermon but as the name of its summit. The Greek and the Aramaic instead date the descent — in the days of Jared — where the Ethiopic locates it.

  • v6 "in the days of Jared" — in Genesis 5:18 Jared is Enoch's father. The name in Hebrew is Yered, from the verb yarad, to come down. The Watchers come down in the days of Descent, and the Aramaic has the same consonants for the name and for the act. It is one of the few wordplays in this book checkable in an original language rather than through a translation — and, like the Hermon one, it is a pun that only exists in the Semitic.

  • v7 "Urakibarameel" — the list has eighteen names. The next verse calls these the chiefs of the tens, and two hundred split into tens needs twenty. This name looks like two run together, which would make nineteen. The count in the text we have does not reach the number the text itself gives.

  • v8 "the chiefs of the two hundred angels — the chiefs of the tens" — the Ge'ez names the whole body of two hundred; the Aramaic gives two ranks, These are the chiefs, and the chief[s] of the ten[s]; the Greek gives only the tens. Three witnesses, three different answers to how the two hundred were organized.

chapters.title: And the Earth Brought Accusation
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 7

1And all the others with them took wives for themselves, each choosing one for himself, and they began to go in to them and to defile themselves with them. And they taught them sorceries and spells, and the cutting of roots, and showed them plants.

2And they became pregnant and bore great giants, whose height was three thousand cubits.

3These consumed all the labor of men, until men could no longer sustain them.

4And the giants turned against them, to devour mankind.

5And they began to sin against the birds and the beasts and the creeping things and the fish, and to devour one another's flesh, and to drink the blood from it.

6Then the earth brought accusation against the lawless ones.

Notes

  • v1 "they taught them sorceries and spells, and the cutting of roots" — the marriages are one sentence; the teaching gets the rest of the verse, and it is what the next chapters return to. The corruption in this book is not chiefly sexual. It is knowledge handed down that was not meant to come down.

  • v2 "three thousand cubits" — about forty-five hundred feet, taller than any mountain in Israel. The number is in the Ge'ez and the Greek alike. Whatever it is, it is not an attempt at a plausible giant.

  • vv3–4 "consumed all the labor of men... then the giants turned against them" — the order matters. First they eat what people produce; only when there is nothing left do they eat the people. The famine comes before the violence, and the text presents that as the natural sequence.

  • v5 "the birds and the beasts and the creeping things and the fish" — the categories of the fifth and sixth days of creation, run through as a list of victims. The giants work backward through what was made.

  • v5 "and to drink the blood from it" — the one prohibition Genesis lays on all humanity after the flood is exactly this: flesh with its life, its blood, you shall not eat (Genesis 9:4). The giants are doing beforehand the single thing the new world will be forbidden.

  • v6 "the earth brought accusation" — the earth is the plaintiff, not the victim. It is the same legal picture as Genesis 4:10, where Abel's blood cries out to God from the ground. In this book the ground itself files the complaint, and chapters 8 and 9 are the case being heard.

  • On the chapter division — the Aramaic fragment begins this chapter with a line the Ge'ez and Greek place at the end of chapter 6: these are the chiefs and the chiefs of the tens. The break between the two chapters sits in a different place in the oldest witness.

  • v6 in the Aramaic — the fragment ends with a vacat: a deliberate blank space left in the scroll. It is a scribe's paragraph mark, still visible on the leather, and it falls exactly where the narrative turns from what the Watchers did to what heaven does about it.

chapters.title: What Azazel Taught
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 8

1And Azazel taught men to make swords of iron and daggers and shields and breastplates of bronze, and showed them the metals of the earth and how to work them, and bracelets and ornaments, and the use of antimony, and the painting of the eyelids, and every kind of costly and choice stone, and all the coloring dyes — and the altering of the world.

2And there was great godlessness, and much fornication, and they went astray, and all their ways became corrupt.

3Shemihazah taught spell-binding and the cutting of roots. Armaros, the undoing of spells. Baraqiel, astrology. Kokabiel, the signs of the stars. Tamiel, the watching of the stars. Asradel, the course of the moon. Shamshiel, the omens of the sun — and they revealed mysteries to their wives.

4And as men were being destroyed, they cried out, and their voice went up to heaven.

Notes

  • v1 the two halves of the list — weapons, and then cosmetics. Swords, daggers, shields, breastplates — and then bracelets, antimony, eye-paint, dyes. The book puts arms and beauty in one breath as the same kind of gift, and the connecting thread is named at the end: metal, dug out of the earth and worked.

  • v1 "swords of iron... breastplates of bronze" — the metals are specified in the Aramaic only. The Ge'ez and Greek both say simply swords and breastplates. The Qumran fragment is the fullest witness here and the oldest, and it also has the gold and the silver being made ready, and stibium and eye-paint by name.

  • v1 "the altering of the world" — the phrase is in the Ge'ez and in neither of the others. It is the verdict the Ethiopic text puts on the whole list.

  • v1 "antimony... the painting of the eyelids" — the black eye-paint of Egyptian and Near Eastern cosmetics, ground from stibium. It is named in all three witnesses, which is a strange thing for three traditions to agree on keeping, and it sits in the same sentence as armor.

  • v3 "Shemihazah taught spell-binding" — the Ge'ez names this teacher Amazarak; the Greek and the Aramaic both name him Shemihazah, the leader from chapter 6. Two witnesses put the chief of the Watchers at the head of the teaching list. One does not.

  • v3 "Shamshiel, the omens of the sun" — from the Aramaic alone, and the name is built on shemesh, the sun. So is the teaching. The Ge'ez and Greek lists stop at the moon.

  • v3 "they revealed mysteries to their wives" — also Aramaic alone, and it closes the loop with 7:1. The wives are not incidental to the corruption. They are who the knowledge was given to.

  • v3 the sciences of the sky — astrology, the signs of the stars, the watching of the stars, the course of the moon, the omens of the sun. Four or five separate specialists, each with a name, all for reading the heavens. For a book that will spend chapters 72–82 on an exact solar calendar, this list is the illegitimate version of its own subject.

  • v4 "their voice went up to heaven" — no one prays. The cry simply rises, the way the earth's accusation simply happened in 7:6. Nothing in these two chapters is addressed to God by anyone on the ground, and heaven answers anyway.

chapters.title: What Ought We to Do?
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 9

1And then Michael and Uriel and Raphael and Gabriel looked down from heaven and saw much blood being shed on the earth, and all the lawlessness being done on the earth.

2And they said to one another, "The sound of their crying — the wasted earth cries out as far as the gates of heaven."

3"And now to you, holy ones of heaven, the souls of men bring their case, saying, 'Bring our judgment before the Most High.'"

4And they said to the Lord, "You are Lord of lords and God of gods and King of kings. The throne of Your glory is for all the generations of eternity, and Your name is holy and glorious for all the generations of eternity, blessed and glorious.

5You made all things, and power over all is with You, and everything is uncovered and open before You, and You see all things, and there is nothing that can be hidden from You.

6See then what Azazel has done — how he taught all unrighteousness on the earth, and revealed the eternal secrets that are kept in heaven, which men were striving to learn.

7And Shemihazah, to whom You gave authority to rule over those who are with him.

8And they went in to the daughters of the men of the earth and slept with them and defiled themselves, and revealed to them all these sins.

9And the women bore giants, and by them the whole earth has been filled with blood and unrighteousness.

10And now — the souls of those who have died cry out and bring their case as far as the gates of heaven, and their groaning has gone up and cannot stop, because of the lawless deeds done on the earth.

11And You know all things before they come to pass, and You see this and their deeds, and You say nothing to us. What ought we to do to them about this?"

Notes

  • v1 the four names — the Greek gives Michael, Uriel, Raphael and Gabriel, and this rendering follows it. The Ge'ez has Michael, Gabriel, Suriel and Uriel. The two lists agree on three names and differ on the fourth, and Suriel and Raphael are not variants of one name — they are different angels. The set of four archangels is not fixed even inside this one book.

  • v2 "the wasted earth cries out" — the cry in chapter 8 went up from men being destroyed. Here it is the earth making the noise. The book keeps giving the ground a voice, and it has done so since 7:6.

  • v3 "bring their case" — the vocabulary through this chapter is legal: a case brought, a judgment requested, a charge laid. The four are being asked to act as advocates, and what they do in vv4–11 is file a brief.

  • v4 the doxology, and what the Greek puts after it — the Greek witness adds a sentence the Ge'ez does not have: Then the Most High commanded the holy archangels, and they bound their leaders and cast them into the abyss until the judgment. In the Greek the sentence of judgment lands here, in the middle of the appeal, before the angels have finished speaking. In the Ge'ez nothing happens until chapter 10. That is a difference in the shape of the story, not in a word.

  • v6 "the eternal secrets that are kept in heaven" — the charge against Azazel is not that he invented anything. It is that what he handed over was already real, and already above. The crime is disclosure.

  • v7 "to whom You gave authority" — the angels point out, carefully, that the ringleader holds his rank by appointment. It is the most pointed sentence in the brief and the shortest.

  • v11 "You say nothing to us" — the Ge'ez ends the appeal there. The Greek is sharper: You see these things and permit them, yet you do not tell us what we ought to do. One witness has the angels complaining that God is silent. The other has them saying He is allowing it.

  • v11 "What ought we to do to them about this?" — the chapter ends on a question from heaven, unanswered, and the four who ask it are the ones who will be given the answer one verse later. The whole appeal is built so that the reader hears the case before the sentence.

chapters.title: Bind Azazel Hand and Foot
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 10

1Then the Most High, the Great and Holy One, spoke, and sent a messenger to the son of Lamech, saying to him:

2"Say to him in My name, 'Hide yourself,' and reveal to him the end that is coming — that the whole earth is perishing, and a flood of water is about to come over the whole earth and destroy everything on it.

3And teach him how he may escape, so that his seed may remain for all the generations of eternity."

4And to Raphael He said, "Bind Azazel hand and foot, and cast him into the darkness. And open the desert that is in Dudael, and cast him there.

5And lay beneath him rough and sharp stones, and cover him with darkness, and let him stay there forever, and cover his face so that he may not see light.

6And on the day of the great judgment he will be led away into the burning fire.

7And heal the earth, which the angels have ruined, and proclaim the healing of the earth — that I may heal it, and that not all the sons of men may perish through the whole mystery that the Watchers disclosed and taught to their sons.

8And the whole earth was laid waste, corrupted by the teaching of the works of Azazel. To him ascribe all sin."

9And to Gabriel the Lord said, "Go against the bastards and the half-breeds and the sons of fornication, and destroy the sons of the Watchers from among men. Send them against one another in a war of destruction, for length of days they do not have.

10And they will all plead with you, but nothing will be granted to their fathers on their behalf — though they hope to live an eternal life, and that each of them may live five hundred years."

11And to Michael He said, "Go, make known to Shemihazah and to the rest with him, who joined themselves to the women to defile themselves with them in their uncleanness,

12and when their sons have slaughtered one another and they have seen the destruction of their beloved ones, bind them for seventy generations under the hills of the earth, until the day of their judgment and their consummation, until the judgment that is forever and ever is finished.

13And in those days they will be led away into the abyss of fire, into the torment and into the prison of eternal confinement.

14And whoever is burned and destroyed from then on will be bound together with them until the end of all generations.

15And destroy all the spirits of the half-breeds and the sons of the Watchers, because they have wronged mankind.

16Destroy all violence from the face of the earth, and let every wicked deed come to an end, and let the plant of righteousness and truth appear — and it will be a blessing, and the works of righteousness and truth will be planted forever with joy.

17And now all the righteous will escape, and they will live until they father thousands, and all the days of their youth and their sabbaths they will complete in peace.

18And in those days the whole earth will be worked in righteousness, and all of it planted with trees, and it will be full of blessing.

19And all the trees of joy will be planted on it, and they will plant vines on it, and the vine planted on it will yield fruit in abundance. And of all the seed sown on it, one measure will produce ten thousand, and one measure of olives will produce ten presses of oil.

20And you — cleanse the earth from all oppression and from all injustice and from all sin and from all godlessness, and wipe out all the uncleanness that is done on the earth.

21And let all the sons of men become righteous, and let all the nations worship and praise Me, and all of them bow down to Me.

22And the earth will be cleansed from all corruption and from all sin and from all plague and from all torment, and I will never again send a flood upon it, for all generations and forever."

Notes

  • v1 "a messenger" — the witnesses name him differently, and one of the names carries meaning. The Greek has Ἰστραήλ, Istrael, which ends in -ēl — El, God, the ending every angel in this book is built on: Michael, Gabriel, Raphael, Uriel, Baraqiel, Kokabiel. And it is one letter from Ἰσραήλ, Israel: a single tau inserted. Israel is the name Jacob is given in Genesis 32:28, explained there as you have striven with God and with men and have prevailed. The Ge'ez has Arsyalalyur, which has no -el ending and no recoverable sense; it looks like a name that has drifted in copying. Whether the Greek preserves a real name or has pulled an unfamiliar one toward a familiar one, nothing in the witnesses decides.

  • v1 "the son of Lamech" — Noah, and the book does not name him. Genesis 5:28–29 has Lamech father a son and call him Noah. Here the man who will survive the flood is identified only by his father, and he never speaks.

  • v4 "Bind Azazel... and open the desert that is in Dudael" — and this is the verse that connects the book to the Day of Atonement. Leviticus 16 has two goats: one for the LORD, and one for Azazel, which is sent away to Azazel, into the wilderness (16:10). The Hebrew Bible never says who or what Azazel is. This book says he is a bound angel in a desert, and puts him there by name.

  • v5 "cover his face so that he may not see light" — the punishment is precisely reversed from the crime. He revealed what was hidden; he is hidden where nothing is revealed to him.

  • v7 "heal the earth" — Raphael's assignment, and his name means God heals. The book gives each of the four a task matching what he is called: Raphael heals, Gabriel (God is my strength) goes to war, Michael (who is like God?) carries the sentence to the chief who overreached.

  • v8 "To him ascribe all sin" — the entire corruption is assigned to one name, in a chapter that has just listed a dozen teachers. The verse reads like a legal finding rather than a description, and it is the sentence the scapegoat ritual enacts: everything laid on one head and sent out.

  • v9 "send them against one another" — the giants are not killed by heaven. They are set to destroy each other, and Gabriel's job is to arrange it. The flood, when it comes, is not what ends them.

  • v10 "each of them may live five hundred years" — set this beside Genesis 6:3, where God says of the same generation his days shall be a hundred and twenty years. Both texts respond to the same crisis with a number, and the numbers do not match.

  • v12 "bind them for seventy generations under the hills" — Jude 6 is this verse: the angels who did not keep their own domain but left their own dwelling, He has kept in eternal chains under darkness for the judgment of the great day. 2 Peter 2:4 says the same and names the place Tartarus. Two New Testament letters describe the punishment of the Watchers, and this is where it is written down.

  • v16 "the plant of righteousness" — the image the book will keep returning to. What replaces the ruined world is not a rescue but a planting, and vv18–19 take it literally: trees, vines, seed, oil.

  • v19 the yields — the Ge'ez says one measure of seed produces ten thousand; the Greek says a thousand. The Ge'ez says one measure of olives gives ten presses; the Greek says ten baths. Both are describing an impossible harvest, and neither agrees with the other on how impossible.

  • v22 "I will never again send a flood upon it" — the promise of Genesis 9:11, spoken here before the flood has happened. The whole chapter is set in the days of Noah and speaks from after them.

chapters.title: The Storehouses of Blessing
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 11

1"And in those days I will open the storehouses of blessing that are in heaven, to send them down upon the earth, upon the work and upon the labor of the sons of men.

2And peace and truth will be joined together for all the days of the world and for all the generations of eternity."

Notes

  • v1 "the storehouses of blessing" — treasuries, granaries: rooms in heaven where something is kept until it is released. The book uses the same picture later for the winds, the snow and the hail, each with its own store. Here what is warehoused is blessing, and the flood chapter ends by opening it.

  • v1 "upon the work and upon the labor of the sons of men" — what is blessed is the working, not the workers. In 7:3 the giants consumed all the labor of men, using the same word for it. The chapter closes the account: what was eaten is repaid.

  • v2 "peace and truth" — the Ge'ez has peace first, the Greek has truth and peace. They are also the two things denied to the Watchers, in this book's standing refrain: there will be no peace for them (5:4, 12:5, 13:1). The two-verse chapter exists to say that what the guilty are refused is given to everyone else.

chapters.title: Enoch the Scribe
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 12

1And before all these things Enoch was taken, and no one among men knew where he was taken, or where he was, or what had become of him.

2And his whole dwelling was with the Watchers and with the holy ones in his days.

3And I, Enoch, was blessing the Lord of majesty and King of the ages. And here — the Watchers called me, Enoch the scribe, and said to me:

4"Enoch, scribe of righteousness, go and declare to the Watchers of heaven — who have left the high heaven and the eternal holy sanctuary, and have defiled themselves with women, and have done as the sons of men do, and have taken wives for themselves, and have worked great ruin on the earth:

5'There will be no peace for you, nor forgiveness of sin.

6And concerning your sons in whom you rejoice — you will see the slaughter of your beloved ones, and you will lament over the destruction of your sons, and you will make supplication forever, but there will be neither mercy nor peace for you.'"

Notes

  • v1 "Enoch was taken, and no one knew where" — Genesis 5:24 says it in six Hebrew words: and Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him. Genesis says it and moves on. This book takes that sentence as its licence: a man removed from the world, unaccounted for, is available to be told things. Everything in these 108 chapters stands on one verse that explains nothing.

  • v1 "before all these things" — the book has just narrated the flood, the binding of Azazel and the renewal of the earth. Now it goes back. The chapter is a hinge: what follows is the part of the story Enoch himself is in.

  • v2 "his dwelling was with the Watchers and with the holy ones" — the same word, Watchers, that names the ones who fell. Not all of them fell. Enoch lives among the wakeful ones, which is why the guilty can reach him and why he can carry a message in either direction.

  • v3 "Enoch the scribe" — the title is the point. He is not a prophet here, and not a priest. He is the one who takes it down, and in v4 the fuller form is scribe of righteousness. In a book about knowledge that was written down and should not have been, the hero's job is writing.

  • v4 "who have left the high heaven and the eternal holy sanctuary" — the Greek word is sanctuary, and it makes heaven a temple and the Watchers its priests. What they have done, in that picture, is walk off their station. Jude 6 puts it the same way: angels who did not keep their own domain but left their own dwelling.

  • v4 "have done as the sons of men do" — the charge is not that they did something monstrous. It is that they did something ordinary. They married and had children, and for them that was the transgression.

  • v5 "There will be no peace for you" — the refrain, and here it is delivered to the Watchers' faces by a man. In 5:4 the same sentence was aimed at human sinners. The book uses one verdict for both.

  • vv5–6 the sentence Enoch carries — no peace, no forgiveness, and then the specific grief: they will watch their own sons killed, and their pleading will not stop and will not work. Chapter 10 ordered the giants to destroy each other; this is what that order looks like from the fathers' side.

  • v3 "the Watchers called me" — worth noticing who initiates. The condemned angels summon the human. In the next chapters they will ask him to write their petition and carry it up for them, and he does. The scribe becomes their advocate.

chapters.title: The Petition of the Watchers
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 13

1And Enoch went and said to Azazel, "There will be no peace for you. A great judgment has gone out against you, to bind you.

2And there will be no relief or mercy or petition for you, because of the wrong you taught, and because of all the works of blasphemy and violence and sin that you showed to the sons of men."

3Then I went and spoke to all of them together, and they were all afraid, and fear and trembling seized them.

4And they asked me to write a record of petition for them, so that they might obtain forgiveness, and that I might carry the record of their petition up before the Lord of heaven —

5because from then on they could not speak, nor lift up their eyes to heaven, for shame at the sins for which they were condemned.

6And then I wrote the record of their petition and their supplication, concerning their spirits and each of their deeds, and concerning what they asked — that there might be forgiveness for them, and forbearance.

7And I went and sat down by the waters of Dan, in the land of Dan, which is south-west of Hermon, and I read out the record of their petition until I fell asleep.

8And here — a dream came to me, and visions fell upon me, and I saw a vision of wrath, and a voice came saying: speak to the sons of heaven and rebuke them.

9And when I woke, I came to them, and they were all sitting gathered together, mourning at Ubelseyael, which is between Lebanon and Senesher, with their faces covered.

10And I spoke before them all the visions I had seen in my sleep, and I began to speak words of righteousness, and to rebuke the Watchers of heaven.

Notes

  • v1 "There will be no peace for you" — the refrain, delivered face to face and to one named angel. It has been said to human sinners (5:4) and to the whole company of Watchers (12:5). Chapter 16 will close the section by repeating it one last time.

  • v4 "they asked me to write a record of petition" — the extraordinary reversal of the book. The fallen angels cannot approach God, so they hire a man as their lawyer. Enoch drafts the appeal, reads it aloud, and carries it up. Chapter 15 will tell him exactly how backwards this is.

  • v5 "they could not speak, nor lift up their eyes" — the reason given is not that they are forbidden. It is shame. Beings who left heaven cannot now look at it.

  • v7 "by the waters of Dan" — a real place: the springs at the foot of Mount Hermon that feed the Jordan, in the territory of the tribe of Dan. The book has put the Watchers on Hermon since 6:6, and it keeps its geography consistent. The Ge'ez says south-west of Hermon; the Greek says to the south of Hermon on the west.

  • v7 "I read out the record... until I fell asleep" — he does not pray it. He reads the document aloud, by water, at the mountain where the oath was sworn, and falls asleep over it. The answer comes as a dream.

  • v8 "and a voice came saying" — the Greek has the voice; the Ge'ez has only the vision of wrath and Enoch's own understanding that he should speak. One witness has him commissioned out loud, the other has him work it out.

  • v9 "mourning at Ubelseyael" — the Ge'ez and the Greek give different forms of both place names: Ubelseyael against Ebelsata, and Senesher against Senisel. Neither place is known from anywhere else. What both agree on is the picture: two hundred angels sitting on the ground between Lebanon and another range, faces covered, waiting for a man to come back with an answer.

chapters.title: The House of Fire and Ice
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 14

1This book is the word of righteousness and the rebuke of the Watchers who are from eternity, as the Holy and Great One commanded in that vision.

2I saw in my sleep what I will now speak with a tongue of flesh and with the breath of my mouth, which the Great One has given to men, to speak with it and to understand with the heart.

3As He created and gave to men the understanding of the word of knowledge, so He created and gave to me the rebuking of the Watchers, the sons of heaven.

4"I wrote down your petition, and in my vision it appeared like this: your petition will not be granted you through all the days of eternity, and the judgment against you is complete and decided.

5And from now on you will not go up into heaven for all eternity, and on earth it has been decreed that you are to be bound for all the days of eternity.

6And before that, you will see the destruction of your beloved sons, and you will have no pleasure in them, and they will fall before you by the sword.

7And your petition on their behalf will not be granted, nor on your own — even while you weep and make supplication, and speak not one word of the writing I wrote."

The Wall of Hail

8And the vision appeared to me like this. Here — clouds called me, and a mist called me, and the courses of the stars and the lightnings hurried me and drove me on, and winds in the vision made me fly and lifted me up and carried me into heaven.

9And I went in until I came near a wall built of stones of hail, and tongues of fire surrounded it, and it began to terrify me.

10And I went into the tongues of fire and came near a great house built of stones of hail. And the walls of that house were like slabs of stone, and all of them were snow, and its floor was snow.

11Its ceiling was like the courses of the stars and the lightnings, and between them were fiery cherubim, and their sky was water.

12And a burning fire was around its walls, and its door burned with fire.

13And I went into that house, and it was hot as fire and cold as ice, and there was nothing of life in it. Fear covered me, and trembling seized me.

14And as I was shaking and trembling, I fell on my face. And I was looking in the vision —

15and here, another house, greater than this one, and its door stood open before me, and it was built entirely of tongues of fire.

16And in every way it surpassed the other in glory and honor and greatness, so that I cannot describe to you its glory and its greatness.

17Its floor was fire, and above it were lightnings and the courses of the stars, and its ceiling also was burning fire.

18And I looked and saw in it a high throne. Its appearance was like crystal, and its wheels like the shining sun, and there was the sound of cherubim.

19And from beneath the throne came streams of flaming fire, and I could not look at it.

20And the Great Glory sat on it, and His robe was brighter than the sun and whiter than any snow.

21And no angel could come in, and no one of flesh could look on the face of the Honored and Glorious One.

22A burning fire was around Him, and a great fire stood before Him, and no one of those around Him came near. Ten thousand times ten thousand were before Him, and He needed no counsel.

23And the holiest of those who drew near to Him did not leave by night or by day, and did not go away from Him.

24And until then I was on my face, covered and trembling. And the Lord called me with His own mouth and said to me, "Come here, Enoch, and hear My word."

25And He raised me up and brought me as far as the door, and I was looking with my face downward.

Notes

  • vv1–3 the book announces itself — a preface in the middle of the story, in Enoch's own voice, saying what the following chapters are. And the claim it makes about itself is modest and strange: a tongue of flesh and the breath of my mouth. He is saying the vision was not speakable, and he is going to speak it anyway.

  • v4 "I wrote down your petition" — the answer to chapter 13. The document Enoch drafted came back refused. Verses 4–7 are him reading the verdict aloud to the angels who hired him.

  • v7 "speak not one word of the writing I wrote" — the petition is not only rejected; they are forbidden to use it. The lawyer is told to instruct his clients that the brief is void.

  • v8 "clouds called me... winds made me fly" — the weather carries him. Nothing in the ascent is an angel or a chariot: cloud, mist, shooting stars, lightning, wind. The same ruach, wind or spirit, that opens seas in Exodus.

  • vv9–13 the first house, of hail and snow and fire — a wall, then a great house, then an inner house. That is a temple plan: outer court, holy place, holy of holies. The building materials are impossible on purpose — it is made of hailstones and snow, and it burns; it is hot as fire and cold as ice in the same sentence.

  • v13 "there was nothing of life in it" — said of the outer house, the one a man can enter. What lies beyond it is where the life is, and he cannot go there yet.

  • v18 "a high throne... its wheels like the shining sun" — Ezekiel 1 has the same furniture: a throne, the appearance of crystal, wheels, cherubim, fire. Whichever came first, the two visions are furnished from the same imagination.

  • vv18–22 and Daniel 7 — set this beside Daniel 7:9–10, which can be checked word for word. Daniel: his garment white as snow; Enoch 14:20: whiter than any snow. Daniel: a river of fire flowing out from before him; Enoch 14:19: streams of flaming fire from beneath the throne. Daniel: a thousand thousands served him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him; Enoch 14:22: ten thousand times ten thousand were before Him. Three specific images, in the same order, in two books.

  • v20 "the Great Glory" — the title used instead of a name. The book will not say God sat on the throne; it says the Glory sat. It is the same move as calling the presence in the wilderness kavod, weight.

  • v22 "He needed no counsel" — that is the Ge'ez. The Greek has something else entirely: his every word was an act. One witness says God takes no advice; the other says God's speech is deed. Both are single short clauses in the same slot, and they are not variants of one another.

  • v25 "And He raised me up" — in the Ge'ez, God does it. In the Greek, one of the holy ones approached me, raised me up, made me stand. Whether a man is lifted to the door of the holy of holies by God's own hand or by an attendant is the sort of thing a tradition decides, and the two traditions decided differently.

speech.text: 1 Enoch 14
This book is the word of righteousness and the rebuke of the Watchers who are from eternity, as the Holy and Great One commanded in that vision.
I saw in my sleep what I will now speak with a tongue of flesh and with the breath of my mouth, which the Great One has given to men, to speak with it and to understand with the heart.

"I wrote down your petition, and in my vision it appeared like this: your petition will not be granted you through all the days of eternity, and the judgment against you is complete and decided.

The Wall of Hail

And the vision appeared to me like this. Here — clouds called me, and a mist called me, and the courses of the stars and the lightnings hurried me and drove me on, and winds in the vision made me fly and lifted me up and carried me into heaven.
And I went in until I came near a wall built of stones of hail, and tongues of fire surrounded it, and it began to terrify me.

And a burning fire was around its walls, and its door burned with fire.
And I went into that house, and it was hot as fire and cold as ice, and there was nothing of life in it. Fear covered me, and trembling seized me.
And as I was shaking and trembling, I fell on my face. And I was looking in the vision —
and here, another house, greater than this one, and its door stood open before me, and it was built entirely of tongues of fire.
And in every way it surpassed the other in glory and honor and greatness, so that I cannot describe to you its glory and its greatness.

And from beneath the throne came streams of flaming fire, and I could not look at it.
And the Great Glory sat on it, and His robe was brighter than the sun and whiter than any snow.
And no angel could come in, and no one of flesh could look on the face of the Honored and Glorious One.
A burning fire was around Him, and a great fire stood before Him, and no one of those around Him came near. Ten thousand times ten thousand were before Him, and He needed no counsel.
And the holiest of those who drew near to Him did not leave by night or by day, and did not go away from Him.
And until then I was on my face, covered and trembling. And the Lord called me with His own mouth and said to me, "Come here, Enoch, and hear My word."
And He raised me up and brought me as far as the door, and I was looking with my face downward.

chapters.title: Where the Evil Spirits Came From
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 15

1And He answered and said to me with His voice, "Hear, and do not be afraid, Enoch, righteous man and scribe of righteousness. Come here and hear My word.

2And go, say to the Watchers of heaven who sent you to petition on their behalf: 'You ought to be petitioning on behalf of men, not men on your behalf.

3Why have you left the high, holy, eternal heaven, and lain with women, and defiled yourselves with the daughters of men, and taken wives for yourselves, and done as the sons of the earth do, and fathered sons who are giants?

4Though you were spirits, holy and living an eternal life, you defiled yourselves with women, and fathered children with the blood of flesh, and lusted with the blood of men, and did as they do — flesh and blood, who die and perish.

5That is why I gave them wives: so that they might sow seed in them, and children be born of them, and so nothing on the earth would be left undone.

6But you were spirits from the beginning, living an eternal life that does not die through all the generations of the world.

7That is why I did not make wives for you. The spirits of heaven — heaven is their dwelling.

The Giants After They Die

8And now, the giants who were born of spirit and flesh will be called evil spirits on the earth, and on the earth will be their dwelling.

9Evil spirits came out from their bodies, because they were created from above. From the holy Watchers is their beginning and their first foundation. They will be evil spirits on the earth, and evil spirits they will be called.

10And the spirits of heaven — in heaven is their dwelling. But the spirits born on the earth — on the earth is their dwelling.

11And the spirits of the giants are clouds that harm: they oppress and corrupt and fall on and fight and crush upon the earth, and cause grief. They eat no food, and they do not thirst, and they are not seen.

12And these spirits will rise up against the sons of men and against the women, because they came out from them.

Notes

  • v2 "You ought to be petitioning on behalf of men, not men on your behalf" — the sentence the whole episode has been built to reach. The angels' job was to carry human prayers up. They have inverted the order of creation so completely that a man is now carrying their prayers, and God's first response to the petition is to point at the direction it is travelling.

  • vv4–7 the argument — and it is an argument, not a decree. Humans were given marriage because they die: children are how a mortal thing continues, and without them the work of the earth would stop. Spirits do not die, so they were not given wives, because they do not need the mechanism. The crime is not lust. It is beings that cannot die using the apparatus of death.

  • v4 "though you were spirits" — the Ge'ez and the Greek both press the contradiction: holy, living, eternal — and then the blood of flesh, the blood of men. The word blood appears three times in one verse, of beings who have none.

  • vv8–9 where demons come from — this is the passage. The giants die; their spirits do not. Born of a spirit father and a human mother, they are unclassifiable: heaven will not take them because they came from flesh, and earth will not release them because they came from above. So they stay here. Everything later literature says about unclean spirits roaming the earth starts in these two verses, and the Hebrew Bible says nothing of the kind anywhere.

  • v8 "will be called evil spirits" — the Ge'ez says evil; the Greek says strong spirits. One letter of difference in the character of the thing being defined.

  • v10 "the spirits of heaven... the spirits born on the earth" — the sorting principle, stated flatly: where you were born is where you belong. It is the same rule that condemns the giants, and it is the only reason given.

  • v11 "they eat no food, and they do not thirst" — the Ge'ez. The Greek says the opposite: eating nothing, but fasting and thirsting. One witness has beings with no appetite; the other has beings in permanent hunger. It is a real disagreement about what a demon is, and the second reading explains the hostility of v12 while the first does not.

  • v12 "these spirits will rise up against the sons of men" — and here the two witnesses contradict each other outright. The Greek reads and they will rise up against the sons of men and against the women. The Ge'ez reads these spirits shall not rise up. A negative particle stands in one and not the other, and the sense of the passage turns on it. This rendering follows the Greek, because v11 has just described what the spirits do to people and chapter 16 goes on to say they will destroy until the last day — the surrounding verses assume the attack.

chapters.title: A Mystery You Should Not Have Known
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 16

1From the day of the slaughter and destruction and death of the giants, the spirits that went out from the souls of their flesh will be destroying without judgment. So they will destroy until the day of the great consummation, when the great age is completed, over the Watchers and the godless.'

2And now, to the Watchers who sent you to petition on their behalf, who were formerly in heaven, say:

3'You were in heaven, and not every mystery had yet been revealed to you — and a mystery that came from God you knew, and this you made known to the women in the hardness of your heart, and through this mystery women and men multiply evil on the earth.'

4Say to them, then: 'You have no peace.'"

Notes

  • v1 "destroying without judgment" — the giants' spirits operate outside the legal order the whole book has been building. The earth brought a case (7:6), the archangels filed a brief (chapter 9), a verdict came down (chapter 10). These spirits are simply loose, and the text says so: no trial governs them until the end.

  • v1 "until the day of the great consummation" — the sentence on the Watchers is bound and dated. The sentence on what they fathered is open-ended. That is the arrangement the book leaves the world in, and it is the reason the story does not end at the flood.

  • v3 "a mystery that came from God you knew" — that is the Greek. The Ge'ez says something close to the reverse: a rejected mystery you knew. On the Greek reading the knowledge was genuine and divine, and the crime was passing it on. On the Ge'ez reading the knowledge was worthless to begin with. The charge against the Watchers changes shape depending on which witness is read.

  • v3 "not every mystery had yet been revealed to you" — even the angels were on a schedule. The crime is not that they knew something, but that they released it early, and to people who had no way to handle it.

  • v3 "in the hardness of your heart" — the phrase used of Pharaoh all through Exodus, turned on angels.

  • v4 "You have no peace" — the fourth and last time. It closes the Watchers section, and after this chapter the book leaves the subject and Enoch begins to travel. The whole trial, from the earth's accusation in 7:6 to this sentence, runs ten chapters and ends on four words.

chapters.title: Where All Flesh Walks
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 17

1And they took me away to a place where those who were there became like burning fire, and when they wished, they appeared like men.

2And they brought me to a dark place, and to a mountain whose summit reached into heaven.

3And I saw the places of the luminaries, and the storehouses of the stars and of the thunders, and into the airy depths, where the bow of fire was, and the arrows and their quivers, and all the lightnings.

4And they took me as far as the waters of life, and as far as the fire of the west, which receives every setting of the sun.

5And we came to a river of fire, in which the fire runs down like water and pours out into a great sea toward the west.

6And I saw the great rivers, and I came as far as the great darkness, and I went where all flesh walks.

7And I saw the winds of the winter darkness, and the pouring out of the abyss of all the waters.

8And I saw the mouth of the earth, of all the rivers, and the mouth of the abyss.

Notes

  • On these chapters — the trial of the Watchers is over. From here to chapter 36 the book is a travelogue: Enoch is taken around the edges of the world and shown how it is put together. What follows is the oldest surviving map of the cosmos in Jewish literature, and it is given as eyewitness report.

  • v1 "became like burning fire, and when they wished, they appeared like men" — the first thing he is shown is not a place but a capacity. These beings have no fixed form; the human shape is one they put on. It is the quiet answer to how two hundred of them married women in chapter 6.

  • v4 "the waters of life" — the Greek has just that. The Ge'ez has the water of life that speaks, a phrase with no parallel and no obvious sense. Something has happened to the line in one tradition or the other, and there is no third witness to break the tie.

  • v5 "a river of fire... pours out into a great sea toward the west" — a river of fire running west into the sea of the dead is the geography of the Greek underworld, where the Pyriphlegethon is literally the blazing-fire river. Whether the book borrowed it or arrived at it independently, this is the furniture of the classical afterlife, described by a Hebrew patriarch.

  • v6 "I went where all flesh walks" — the plainest phrase in the chapter and the darkest. Not a country and not a name: the road everyone is on. The book has been describing storehouses and mountains, and then in eight words says he visited death.

  • v7–8 "the mouth of the abyss" — the chapter ends at plumbing. Every river has a mouth, and so does the abyss, and Enoch has been shown where the water comes from and where it goes. The interest is not moral here; it is mechanical. Somebody wanted to know how the world works.

chapters.title: The Prison of the Stars
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 18

1And I saw the storehouses of all the winds, and I saw that with them He ordered the whole creation and the foundations of the earth. And I saw the cornerstone of the earth.

2And I saw the four winds that bear the earth and the firmament of heaven.

3And I saw how the winds stretch out the height of heaven, and they stand between heaven and earth. They are the pillars of heaven.

4And I saw the winds that turn the heaven, that bring the disk of the sun and all the stars to their setting.

5And I saw the winds upon the earth bearing the clouds, and I saw the paths of the angels. I saw at the edge of the earth the firmament of heaven above.

6And I passed on toward the south, and it burns day and night, where the seven mountains are of precious stone — three facing east and three facing south.

7And those toward the east were of colored stone, and one was of pearl, and one of healing stone. And those toward the south were of red stone.

8And the middle one reached up to heaven, like the throne of God, of alabaster stone, and the summit of the throne was of sapphire.

9And I saw a burning fire. And beyond these mountains

10is a place at the end of the great earth. There the heavens come to an end.

11And I saw a great chasm among the pillars of heavenly fire, and I saw pillars of fire descending among them, without measure, neither toward the height nor toward the depth.

12And beyond that chasm I saw a place where there was no firmament of heaven above it, and no foundation of earth beneath it, and no water on it, and no birds — but it was a desolate and terrible place.

13I saw there seven stars, like great burning mountains. And when I asked about them,

14the angel said, "This is the place of the end of heaven and earth. It has become a prison for the stars of heaven and for the host of heaven.

15And the stars that roll over the fire — these are the ones that transgressed the command of the Lord at the beginning of their rising, because they did not come out at their appointed times."

16And He was angry with them, and bound them until the time when their sin is completed.

Notes

  • v1 "the storehouses of all the winds" — the same word used in 11:1 for the storehouses of blessing. The book's picture of heaven is a warehouse with rooms: blessing in one, wind in another, and later snow, hail and dew in their own. Nothing in the weather is loose.

  • v1 "the cornerstone of the earth" — the building term. Job 38:6 asks who laid the cornerstone of the earth and gets no answer. Enoch says he saw it.

  • vv2–3 "the four winds that bear the earth... they are the pillars of heaven" — the winds are not weather here; they are structural. They hold the earth up, hold the sky apart from it, and turn the sky at v4. This is a working model, and the moving part is air.

  • v8 "like the throne of God, of alabaster... the summit of sapphire" — the middle mountain of seven, reaching to heaven, described as a throne. Exodus 24:10 has the elders see under God's feet something like a pavement of sapphire, and Ezekiel 1:26 puts a throne of sapphire above the firmament. The stone is consistent across three books.

  • v10 "there the heavens come to an end" — that is the Greek. The Ge'ez says something else entirely: there the waters gather together. One witness ends the sky at this point; the other pools the sea here.

  • vv12–16 the prison for stars — and this is the book's strangest judgment. Seven stars are locked up, and the charge in v15 is that they did not come out at their appointed times. Not rebellion, not pride. Lateness. They broke schedule.

  • v15 against chapter 2 — the opening of the book told the reader to observe the lights in heaven, how they do not change their paths (2:1), and built its whole case against humanity on the contrast. Chapter 18 shows what happens to the lights that do change. The argument turns out to have teeth on both sides.

  • v13 who asks the question — in the Greek, Enoch asks about the seven stars. In the Ge'ez it is the reverse: a spirit questioned me. A small clause, and the two traditions put the interrogation in opposite directions.

  • v16 "until the time when their sin is completed" — the Ge'ez adds in the year of mystery; the Greek says ten thousand years. One tradition gives the sentence a number and the other makes its length the point of not knowing.

chapters.title: Their Wives Will Become Sirens
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 19

1And Uriel said to me, "Here the angels who mingled with women will stand, and their spirits, taking many different forms, defile mankind and will lead them astray to sacrifice to demons as gods — until the day of the great judgment, in which they will be judged until they are finished.

2And their wives, the wives of the angels who went astray, will become sirens."

3And I, Enoch, alone saw the vision, the ends of all things. And no one among men will see as I have seen.

Notes

  • v1 "to sacrifice to demons as gods" — the book's explanation of where idolatry comes from. Not carved wood and not mistake: the spirits of the fallen angels take shapes and are worshiped in them. Every god of the nations, on this account, is a Watcher in costume.

  • v1 "taking many different forms" — picking up 17:1, where beings became fire or men when they wished. The shapelessness that made chapter 6 possible is what makes idolatry possible.

  • v2 "will become sirens" — the Greek word is σειρῆνας, seirēnas, and it is exactly the word Homer uses. There is no Semitic creature behind it; the sirens are Greek, from the Odyssey, women whose singing draws sailors onto rocks. The Ge'ez keeps the word too. A Jewish book about the sons of Seth and the daughters of men ends its account of the Watchers' wives by turning them into a Greek myth, and every surviving witness preserves it. Whatever else this tells us, it dates the world the book was written in.

  • v2 the women's fate — the men's spirits become demons (15:8–9) and the women become sirens. The book gives the wives a punishment of their own and it is the only sentence in the whole episode about what happened to them.

  • v3 "I, Enoch, alone saw" — the chapter ends by closing the door. He is not reporting something others could check. It is the standard claim of this kind of writing, and stating it plainly is the honest thing the text does.

chapters.title: The Names of the Archangels
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 20

1And these are the names of the holy angels who watch:

2Uriel, one of the holy angels, who is over the world and over Tartarus.

3Raphael, one of the holy angels, who is over the spirits of men.

4Raguel, one of the holy angels, who takes vengeance on the world of the luminaries.

5Michael, one of the holy angels, who is set over the best part of mankind, and over the nation.

6Saraqael, one of the holy angels, who is set over the spirits that sin in the spirit.

7Gabriel, one of the holy angels, who is over paradise and the serpents and the cherubim.

Notes

  • The list says seven and names six. The Greek closes the chapter with the words names of the seven archangels — ἀρχαγγέλων ὀνόματα ἑπτά — and only six are given, in both witnesses. This is the same kind of countable gap as chapter 6, where eighteen names were listed for twenty chiefs of tens. Later manuscripts and later tradition supply a seventh, Remiel; neither of our witnesses has him here.

  • v2 "over Tartarus" — the Greek is ταρτάρου, Tartarus, the deepest pit of the Greek underworld, below Hades. It is not a Hebrew idea and there is no Hebrew word behind it. It is also the word 2 Peter 2:4 reaches for — the only place in the New Testament that uses it — in the verse about angels who sinned being cast down and kept for judgment. The letter describing the Watchers' punishment uses this book's vocabulary for the place.

  • v2 Uriel's brief — the Ge'ez gives him thunder and trembling; the Greek gives him the world and Tartarus. That is not a variant spelling. It is two different jobs, and the Greek's is far larger.

  • v5 Michael "over the nation" — the Ge'ez. The Greek has him over the chaos. Michael as the guardian of Israel is how Daniel 12:1 knows him — Michael, the great prince who stands over the sons of your people — so the Ge'ez reading is the one the rest of the Bible recognizes.

  • v6 "Saraqael" — the Ge'ez form; the Greek has Sariel. And Sariel is one of the four archangels in the Ge'ez list back at 9:1, where the Greek had Raphael instead. The names in this tradition move around.

  • v7 "over paradise and the serpents and the cherubim" — three things in one portfolio, and they are the three things standing in Genesis 3: the garden, the serpent, and the cherubim placed at the gate. Gabriel's job description is a summary of the chapter that put humanity outside.

  • the names themselves — every one ends in -el, God. Uri-el, my light is God. Rapha-el, God heals. Micha-el, who is like God. Gabri-el, God is my strength. The names are not labels; they are sentences, and each angel's task in this list matches the sentence he is called by.
